reason: The sources provide 16 atomic claims documented by multiple sites, including the striking details of the premature victory medals and the failed siege logistics.
story: In 1741, Admiral Edward Vernon arrived at Cartagena de Indias with a massive British fleet, certain of an easy victory. Back in London, the public was so convinced of triumph that they began celebrating before the battle was over. Manufacturers minted thousands of commemorative medals; some even depicted the Spanish defender, Blas de Lezo, kneeling in submission to Vernon. But the reality was a nightmare. De Lezo, a veteran nicknamed 'Half-Man' for his missing eye, arm, and leg, outmaneuvered the British. While Vernon and his land commander, Thomas Wentworth, were paralyzed by mutual hatred, their troops were decimated by yellow fever. A final, desperate night assault on the city's fort ended in disaster when British soldiers found their scaling ladders were ten feet too short. The British eventually retreated in disgrace, leaving behind 18,000 dead. The propaganda medals remained as permanent reminders of a hubristic defeat that eventually collapsed the British government.
angle: Admiral Vernon was so certain of victory that medals were minted in London showing the Spanish commander kneeling before him, even as the British fleet was being decimated by disease and a botched assault using ladders that were 10 feet too short.

claims.claim: The conflict began over an incident where Robert Jenkins' ear was severed by Spanish coast guards.

evidence.quote: claimed a Spanish coast guard officer had severed his ear.
had part of his ear severed by Spanish coast guards searching his ship for contraband.

claims.claim: The battle is known as part of the War of Jenkins' Ear.

evidence.quote: took place during the 1739 to 1748 War of Jenkins' Ear
Also known as the War of Jenkins' Ear, this conflict had its origin in April 1731

claims.claim: The Spanish defense was commanded by Admiral Blas de Lezo, who had lost an eye, an arm, and a leg.

evidence.quote: one-eyed, one-legged and one-armed Spanish admiral Blas de Lezo.
city’s defence was commanded by the one-eye, one-hand, one-legged Admiral Blas de Lezo.

claims.claim: Admiral Vernon sent early reports of his entry into the bay to King George, signaling an imminent victory.

evidence.quote: Vernon dispatched a messenger, Captain Laws, to Britain to inform King George of the British forces' entry to the inner bay
Vernon had sent a messenger to inform King George of the British forces' entry to the inner bay.

claims.claim: British manufacturers rushed to produce medals celebrating the victory before it was actually achieved.

evidence.quote: The British, certain that they were going to take the victory, had rushed to mint coins and medals to celebrate it.
more medals were produced in commemoration of this 'victory.'

claims.claim: One medal design depicted Blas de Lezo kneeling before the victorious Admiral Vernon.

evidence.quote: Admiral Vernon was shown looking down upon the 'defeated' Spanish admiral Don Blas de Lezo who appeared kneeling down.
One, erect and victorious, that of Admiral Vernon. The other, kneeling and imploring, is identified as 'Don Blas'

claims.claim: The night assault on the fort failed partly because the scaling ladders brought by the British were too short.

evidence.quote: Those ladders brought forward were too short by 10 feet (3 m).
The ladders were too short

claims.claim: The British fleet was massive, consisting of around 180 to 195 ships.

evidence.quote: one hundred and ninety-five ships and around thirty thousand men
with over 180 ships and 30,000 men

claims.claim: Contempt and lack of cooperation between Admiral Vernon and General Wentworth hindered the campaign.

evidence.quote: De Lezo was aided by the contempt that Vernon and Wentworth had for each other
Vernon and Wentworth did not get along

claims.claim: The British suffered thousands of deaths, with the majority caused by disease.

evidence.quote: suffered over 9,500–11,500 fatalities, in great part to disease
15,000 British soldiers and sailors were killed (many due to disease)

claims.claim: The expedition and battle lasted for a total of 67 days before the British withdrew.

evidence.quote: The expedition and battle lasted for 67 days and ended with the British fleet withdrawing in defeat
After 67 days of fighting, Vernon finally decided to call off the siege of Cartagena.

claims.claim: Admiral Vernon is credited with the origin of 'grog' by ordering rum to be diluted with water.

evidence.quote: The origin of the name "grog" for rum diluted with water is attributed to Vernon.
Grog became the name for the watered down rum served in the Navy after the Admiral who introduced it.

claims.claim: The news of the disaster at Cartagena led to the collapse of Robert Walpole's government.

evidence.quote: Following the news of the disaster Robert Walpole's government soon collapsed.
failed assault caused the collapse of Robert Warpole’s government

disputed: The exact number of ships in the British fleet varies between sources (124 in S1, 186 or 195 in S2, and 180 in S4).
The total British death toll is cited as 18,000 (S1), 15,000 (S4), or 4,500 (S2); the script should attribute the higher numbers to combined casualties of combat and disease.
The legend of Robert Jenkins presenting his ear directly to the House of Commons is described by S1 as having no basis in fact, though S4 states he presented it to Parliament.
A rumored exchange of letters between Vernon and de Lezo is dismissed by S1 as having no evidence.
